ACTIVITY 1  EXPLORE THE ECOSYSTEM
Mission 1 • Investigate first • Suggested learning time 3 hours
WHAT YOU WILL ACHIEVE

Investigate the teacher-approved garden, map its main features, measure a selected bed and record starting conditions. You will finish with a labelled habitat map and one question to investigate next. Planting and insect counts come later.
ROLE
PRACTICAL RESPONSIBILITY
Observer
Notice plants, flowers, shade and disturbance from the path.
Measurer
Measure accessible edges with a teammate holding the tape.
Mapper
Sketch the layout and agree symbols with the team.
Recorder and reporter
Write observations, label uncertainty and explain findings.
Rotate roles during the session. Each student measures or checks one feature and adds one labelled observation to the shared map.
SAFETY  Measure from clear paths. Do not stretch across beds, disturb nests or enter restricted areas.
START HERE  Find the agreed garden boundary. Read the five map steps, then take a measuring turn. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Your map has units, a key and one observation you checked at the site.
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 1  FIVE STEPS TO A SITE MAP
Observe → measure → record → explain → improve
1  AGREE THE BOUNDARY  |  20 MIN
Walk the approved route with your teacher. Identify where you may work and where you must not enter. Select one manageable bed or patch. Draw the boundary before recording details.
2  OBSERVE AND SKETCH  |  35 MIN

From the path, sketch beds, paths, flowering plants, the tap and shaded areas. Mark north if you can establish it reliably; otherwise mark direction as not checked. Record date, time and current weather.
One feature I labelled is ____________________________.
3  MEASURE AND CHECK  |  35 MIN

Measure accessible length and width with a teammate. Record metres or centimetres consistently. If a bed is rectangular, estimate area as length × width. For an irregular bed, sketch it without pretending this formula gives its exact area.
Our measurement and units are ______________________.
4  RECORD WHAT YOU KNOW  |  35 MIN

Record plants with visible open flowers and signs of human disturbance. Mark unknown plant names for later checking. Distinguish “I saw” from “I think”. A single visit cannot establish daily sunlight hours.
5  CHECK AND PLAN A RETURN  |  35 MIN

Compare the sketch with the garden. Add a key and an accessible observation spot. Ask the teacher to check the map. Plan a return visit at another agreed time to check shade. Discuss how a gardener might use the map. Share one question for Activity 2.
FINAL 20 MIN  Complete the short log and five thinking questions; receive teacher feedback. Total suggested learning time: 180 minutes.
DIGITAL CHECK  If taking a photo, follow school permission rules and keep student faces and identifying details out of the evidence image.

POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 2  MEET THE FLOWER VISITORS
Mission 2 • Notice clues • Suggested learning time 3 hours

Your map from Activity 1 shows where to work. Now observe animals visiting flowers in that patch. Use visible clues to suggest a broad group, describe what the visitor does and record uncertainty. These practice records prepare us for consistent measurements in Activity 4.
TOP LEFT  Bee-like visitor
TOP RIGHT  Butterfly-like visitor
BOTTOM LEFT  Fly-like visitor
BOTTOM RIGHT  Beetle-like visitor
Illustrative AI-generated examples; actual local visitors may look different. Images help you ask questions, not confirm a species or prove pollination.
WHAT YOU WILL ACHIEVE
Create a flower-visitor observation sheet, explain the clues behind each suggested group and choose one uncertain record to check. A visit to a flower is not proof that pollen was transferred.
GET READY  Bring your site map, clipboard, pencil, clock and a teacher-selected field guide. An optional school-approved camera can record a visitor without approaching it.
SAFETY  Observe from the path. Do not catch, touch, chase or feed insects. If a visitor is too close or you feel unsafe, step back and tell the teacher.

START HERE  Use the same approved patch. Observe without touching insects; describe what you can see before naming a visitor. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Your record separates a checked identification from “unknown”; do not guess to fill a box.
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 2  FIVE OBSERVATION STEPS
Watch carefully • Describe first • Check before naming
1  RETURN TO OUR PATCH  |  20 MIN
Use the approved spot on your map. Check the path, weather and comfort with the teacher. Choose a visible group of flowers. Record the patch name, date, time and current weather.
2  PRACTISE READING CLUES  |  30 MIN

Study the reference pictures or a teacher-selected guide. Notice body shape, visible wings, antennae and behaviour. Similar colours can occur in different groups. Use “bee-like”, “fly-like” or “unknown” when the evidence is limited.
3  WATCH WITHOUT DISTURBING  |  40 MIN

Make two 10-minute practice watches with a break and role rotation between them. Use the remaining time to set up and discuss what you noticed. Describe a landing on a flower, movement between flowers or resting nearby. Stay in place rather than following a visitor.
4  MAKE AN HONEST RECORD  |  35 MIN

Write one row per observation. Add a visible clue and behaviour, then mark your suggested group as tentative or checked with help. You may see the same insect again; the rows are not a count of different animals or species. Record “none seen” when appropriate.
5  COMPARE AND CHECK  |  35 MIN

Compare notes with a teammate. Choose one unclear record and check it with the teacher, a suitable guide or an invited local expert. Keep the first description and add what changed. Share one question about flower visitors for Activity 3.
FINAL 20 MIN  Complete the five thinking questions, review your evidence and agree a next step. Suggested total: 180 minutes, with indoor preparation and reflection included.
DIGITAL CHECK  Search only with teacher guidance. Do not upload student faces or location details. Treat an image-search or AI identification as a suggestion to verify.

POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 3  INVESTIGATE POLLINATION
Mission 3 • Build a model • Suggested learning time 3 hours

In Activity 2 we observed flower visitors. Now we will model one possible route by which an animal carries pollen. Build two flower cards and a paper visitor, compare a no-transfer trial with a transfer trial, then explain what the model can and cannot show.
WHAT YOU WILL ACHIEVE

Make a labelled model, perform the transfer yourself, record what reaches the target and explain why a flower visit alone does not prove pollination. Keep your Activity 2 observation sheet nearby to connect the model with a real question.
OUR PRACTICAL OUTCOME  Two flower cards, one paper carrier, a trial record and a clear explanation of pollen transfer.
SAFETY  Use large paper dots, not real pollen, powders or glitter. Do not collect insects or pick school flowers without permission. Use scissors only as demonstrated.

START HERE  Read the model instructions and decide who will move, observe and record the model pollen. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Explain what your model represents and one way a real flower is different.
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
UNDERSTAND THE MODEL
Real flower parts • Classroom representations • Clear limits
THE IDEA WE ARE MODELLING

An anther produces pollen. A stigma is the flower part that receives pollen. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. Our cards represent two flowers of the same plant species; we use a paper visitor to model animal-assisted transfer.
MATERIAL
USE IN OUR MODEL
Two card sheets and coloured paper
Make and label flower A and flower B.
Large yellow paper dots
Represent pollen. Use a teacher-agreed number, such as 6.
Folded paper visitor with an open pocket
Carry the paper dots between the cards.
Glue stick or tape and a marker
Secure model parts; label source, carrier and target.
Tray, pencil and recording sheet
Contain loose dots and record both trials.
WHAT THIS MODEL DOES NOT SHOW

Moving paper dots does not show living pollen, pollinator behaviour, fertilisation, seed formation or successful plant reproduction. In nature pollen can cling to an animal; our pocket and hands are classroom substitutes. An observer must look for real evidence before making a claim.
Which model part represents the visitor’s role? Which part is only a classroom convenience?
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 3  FIVE PICTURE STEPS
Prepare → predict → compare → transfer → explain
PICTURE
WHAT TO DO

1  MAKE TWO FLOWER CARDS  |  35 MIN Draw or make flowers A and B on separate cards. Label a source area on A “anthers” and a target circle on B “stigma”. Place the agreed number of dots in the source. The cards represent the same plant species.

2  BUILD THE PAPER VISITOR  |  25 MIN Draw a butterfly or other visitor on card. Fold a short paper strip into an open pocket and tape its sides to the carrier. Ask the teacher to demonstrate the fold. Check that the dots fit and can be removed.

3  TRY THE NO-TRANSFER COMPARISON  |  25 MIN Reset B so its target has no dots. Leave all dots on A and do not move the carrier or dots between cards. Observe and record the target. This is our classroom comparison, not a trial with a real flower.

4  MODEL A TRANSFER  |  40 MIN Reset both cards. Load some source dots into the paper visitor’s pocket. Move it from A to B and place the carried dots on the target. Rotate roles and reset for each student’s turn. Keep a row for every transfer trial.

5  CHECK AND EXPLAIN  |  35 MIN Record source dots, dots on the target and dots elsewhere or remaining. Compare the two kinds of trial. Explain how the model represents pollen transfer and name one important limitation. Pack away all dots.
FINAL 20 MIN  Complete the five questions and receive feedback. Total suggested learning time: 180 minutes.
DIGITAL CHECK  If you research a flower or visitor, check the source with your teacher. Label a photo of your work “classroom model” when sharing with school permission.

NEXT  Activity 4 — Measure Consistently. We will agree a repeatable way to observe flower visits and establish baseline records before changing our habitat.
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 4  MEASURE CONSISTENTLY
Mission 4 • Establish our baseline • Suggested learning time 3 hours

Our map, visitor descriptions and pollination model help us ask a better question: how can we record flower visits in a repeatable way? Agree a counting rule and complete three valid 10-minute watches before making habitat changes. These starting records are our baseline.
WHAT YOU WILL ACHIEVE

Produce a clear observation protocol, three timed records and a short explanation of variation. We count visit events under our rule. We are not counting unique insects, identifying every species or measuring successful pollination.
GET READY  Bring your site map, clipboard, pencil, clock and visitor reference from Activity 2. Choose a small patch that one observer can watch from a safe spot.
SAFETY  Stay on the approved path. Do not move plants or approach insects to make counting easier. Stop if weather or visitor behaviour makes the watch unsafe.

START HERE  Find the agreed patch and observation method. Keep the observation duration and counting rule consistent. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  A partner can repeat your method from the written patch, duration and conditions.
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
OUR REPEATABLE COUNTING RULE
A classroom protocol • Agree it before recording
SITUATION
WHAT WE RECORD
Arrives from outside and lands on a flower in the patch
One visit. Record a broad group or unknown.
Moves between flowers while staying inside the patch
No extra visit under this rule.
Leaves the patch, then returns and lands on a flower
A new visit event; it may be the same insect.
Already present when the watch begins
Note present at start; do not count its existing visit.
Flies through or rests only on a leaf
Do not count as a flower visit.
Identity is unclear
Record unknown; do not guess.
No visits during a complete valid watch
Record zero, with the conditions.
Interrupted or unable to observe the whole patch
Mark invalid; keep the reason and repeat a full watch later.
KEEP THE METHOD THE SAME

Use the same patch boundary, observation spot, 10-minute duration and rule. For repeat visits, aim for a similar time window and record actual time, weather, observer and number of open flowers or flower heads. Choose one flower-count unit and use it throughout. Do not pool two observers’ counts.

Your teacher may adapt this classroom protocol before baseline collection. Record the final rule and keep it for follow-up watches. If a rule must change later, note the break and collect a comparable new baseline.
Why is “visits” a more accurate label than “number of pollinators” for these records?
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 4  FIVE FIELDWORK STEPS
Agree → practise → watch → check → summarise
1  DEFINE OUR PATCH  |  25 MIN

Use the Activity 1 map. Agree a small visible boundary and a safe fixed observation spot. Count open flowers or flower heads using one agreed unit. Write the rule and patch reference before the watches.
2  CALIBRATE OUR RULE  |  30 MIN

Practise briefly with two classmates counting independently. Compare disagreements and discuss which event qualified. Keep the practice separate from baseline data. Everyone practises observing, timing and recording.
3  COMPLETE THREE WATCHES  |  60 MIN

Allow three full 10-minute watches plus setup, breaks and role rotation. One named observer calls each visit; one recorder makes a tally; one timekeeper signals start and end; a checker records conditions. Rotate practical roles between watches and note observer changes.
4  CHECK DATA QUALITY  |  25 MIN

Add tallies by visitor group and check the total. Confirm each watch lasted 10 minutes without a gap. Keep interrupted records with their reason; do not treat them as zero or silently shorten them. Repeat a full valid watch when school conditions allow.
5  SUMMARISE THE BASELINE  |  20 MIN

Compare valid watches using a small table or graph. If the method and patch are the same, calculate the mean recorded visits per 10-minute watch. State conditions and limits. Ask how a gardener might use these records alongside flowering and care information.
FINAL 20 MIN  Complete the five questions and receive feedback. Total suggested learning time: 180 minutes. Teachers can spread watches across agreed sessions and record time actually used.
DIGITAL CHECK  Use a school-approved spreadsheet if helpful. Keep raw tallies and label missing data. Share only with school permission; omit student contact and location details.

Five questions • Use your records and the agreed rule

2. Why should all watches use the same duration, boundary and counting rule?
3. How is a valid zero different from a watch interrupted halfway through?

POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 5  IDENTIFY HABITAT GAPS
Mission 5 • Use evidence before choosing an improvement

You have mapped the garden, observed visitors and collected a baseline. Now review what the habitat already provides and what may need improvement. Combine your records with a careful site audit and a conversation with the gardener or another suitable local resource person.
WHAT YOU WILL ACHIEVE

Produce a short habitat audit and a justified priority for Activity 6. Separate observed facts, possible explanations and unanswered questions. A low visit count alone does not tell us what is missing or what caused it.
GET READY  Bring the Activity 1 map, Activity 2 visitor sheet, Activity 4 baseline and protocol, clipboard and pencil. Prepare questions before a teacher-arranged conversation.
SAFETY  Observe from agreed paths. Do not move logs, clear bare soil, remove plants or disturb shelter to inspect it. Report urgent hazards to the teacher immediately.

START HERE  Open your map and observation records. Choose one habitat gap supported by something you actually recorded. CHECK BEFORE MOVING ON  Explain the evidence for the gap and what still needs checking before choosing plants.
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
READ OUR HABITAT WITH CARE
Look for strengths as well as possible gaps
WHAT TO REVIEW
EVIDENCE TO COLLECT
WHAT TO AVOID ASSUMING
Flowers and flowering periods
Which plants have open flowers on each recorded date? What does the gardener know about other months?
One visit describes the whole year.
Plant suitability and site conditions
Existing plant names where checked, light observations, space and local advice.
Any attractive plant will suit this site.
Shelter and undisturbed areas
Map shrubs and areas that staff already leave undisturbed; observe without moving materials.
Bare ground or leaf litter is always waste.
Human activity and care
Record trampling or disturbance seen; ask staff about watering, mowing and maintenance.
A practice occurred just because you suspect it.
Practical care and access
Who can maintain an improvement? Is there an accessible route and suitable approved space?
A feature will look after itself.
Visitor records
Use valid counts, actual dates, conditions and uncertainties from earlier work.
Fewer recorded visits prove the cause or show all pollinators are absent.
ASK BEFORE MAKING A CLAIM

Use three labels: OBSERVED = recorded directly; REPORTED = told by a person or source; TO CHECK = still uncertain. Date each record and name the source by role, such as school gardener. A useful audit can conclude that more evidence is needed.
EXAMPLE ONLY  The trail above illustrates reasoning. It is not evidence from your school and does not establish that a particular plant is needed.
POLLINATOR PARADISE  •  CLASS 8 COMPOSITE SKILL LAB
ACTIVITY 5  FIVE AUDIT STEPS
Review → inspect → consult → compare → justify
1  REVIEW OUR EVIDENCE  |  25 MIN
Lay out the map, visitor notes and baseline. Each student identifies one strength, one possible concern and one uncertainty, citing a page, row or date. Keep invalid watches separate.
2  WALK THE APPROVED ROUTE  |  35 MIN

Return to the same area with your teacher. Observe flowers, existing shelter, human activity and access from the path. Mark locations on your map. Record facts without changing the habitat. Everyone adds a labelled observation.
3  CONSULT A LOCAL WORKER  |  35 MIN

Ask the school gardener, grounds staff or another teacher-approved resource person about flowering periods, local plant suitability and maintenance. Record their role, date and advice. If no person is available, prepare questions and mark them pending.
4  COMPARE POSSIBLE PRIORITIES  |  35 MIN

Compare two concerns using evidence, likely usefulness, feasible care and school permission. Identify what still needs checking. Do not give an unsupported concern a higher priority simply because it sounds impressive.
5  JUSTIFY OUR NEXT INVESTIGATION  |  30 MIN

Choose one priority to explore in Activity 6, or explain why you need another observation first. Say what you would retain and protect. Ask the teacher to check your reasoning; purchasing and planting decisions come later.
FINAL 20 MIN  Complete the five thinking questions and receive feedback. Total suggested learning time: 180 minutes. Arrange any conversation within the teacher-agreed schedule.
DIGITAL CHECK  Check online plant advice with local guidance. Record source and date; do not publish a worker’s photo, contact details or conversation recording without permission.
